23 Which row could describe electromagnetic waves?
type of wave
speed in free space
A
longitudinal
faster for shorter wavelengths
B
longitudinal
the same for all wavelengths
C
transverse
faster for shorter wavelengths
D
transverse
the same for all wavelengths

hints: Look at the first column: check whether the oscillations in an electromagnetic wave are parallel to or perpendicular to the direction of energy travel.
Recall what oscillates in an electromagnetic wave - electric and magnetic fields - and how that allows polarisation, a property only of transverse waves.
Recall the free-space speed $c$ in $v = f\lambda$: in vacuum $c$ is fixed, so a shorter $\lambda$ means a higher $f$, not a higher $v$.
walkthrough: Identify the two tests in the table: type of wave means longitudinal versus transverse, and speed in free space means whether $v$ depends on wavelength $\lambda$.
State the rule for type: electromagnetic waves are oscillations of electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to the direction of propagation, so they are transverse and can be polarised.
This eliminates the longitudinal rows, leaving only the transverse rows to consider.
State the rule for speed: in free space all electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma, travel at the same speed $c \approx 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Use $c = f\lambda$ to see the cause-and-effect: if $c$ is constant then shorter $\lambda$ gives larger $f$, not larger $c$. So the speed is the same for all wavelengths.
Combining transverse with same speed for all wavelengths matches the row with transverse and the same for all wavelengths. This is option D

A.explanation: Electromagnetic waves are not longitudinal and their free-space speed does not increase for shorter wavelengths.

B.explanation: The speed part is correct but electromagnetic waves are not longitudinal with oscillations parallel to travel.

C.explanation: The transverse part is correct but in free space all wavelengths travel at the same speed $c$, not faster when $\lambda$ is shorter.

D.explanation: Electromagnetic waves are transverse and all travel at $c \approx 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in free space, independent of wavelength.
